title: Late Edo Japanese Temporal Clock
intro: The late Edo model divides computed daylight and darkness into six unequal seasonal toki each, displaying a traditional branch name and bell count.
structure: Day: U (6), Tatsu (5), Mi (4), Uma (9), Hitsuji (8), Saru (7). Night: Tori (6), Inu (5), I (4), Ne (9), Ushi (8), Tora (7). Each period is one sixth of the current day or night span; its duration changes with season and location.
example: If computed dawn and dusk are 05:00 and 19:00 in apparent solar time, each daylight toki lasts 140 ordinary minutes. The first is U, six bells; at 07:20 it advances to Tatsu, five bells. The night toki in this illustrative example last 100 minutes.
history: Japanese seasonal clocks used unequal day and night hours and descending bell counts. The late Edo profile distinguishes dawn and dusk by a solar depression of 7 degrees 21 minutes 40 seconds, unlike the earlier fixed 36-minute extension.
model: Compute apparent solar phase and symmetric dawn/dusk boundaries using solar declination, latitude and the specified depression angle. Divide the day or wrapped night span into six equal parts, select the zero-based index and localised branch/bell notation. The provider searches the next rendered boundary.
limits: The seconds option does not create subdivisions. Requires valid coordinates; undefined crossings produce N/A. The model uses compact modern astronomy, not direct Edo observations or a universal historical locality. The solar model assumes an idealised sea-level horizon and standard depression; local terrain and weather are not modelled.
